title: Guide to molecular databases, phylogenetics and molecular evolution
author: Florian G Jacques
materials: This is a step-by-step protocol for non-bioinformatic users to reconstruct the phylogeny and evolution of genes or proteins. Studying molecular evolution consists in gathering sequences and reconstructing the phylogenetic tree to retrace the evolution of these sequences. Based on a recently published up-to-date protocol for phylogenetic analysis (Jermiin et al. , 2020), we propose a simple guide to the study of molecular evolution, from molecular databases to phylogenetic analysis and diverse aspects of molecular evolution. This guide is especially intended to students and researchers who are not familiar with evolutionary biology and bioinformatics. We further illustrate our protocol with two test-case studies on the evolution of human p53 (TP53) and Cyclins/CDKs protein families, and provide instructions and codes. This guide includes: A brief introduction to phylogenetic analysis presenting concepts and definitions, A compilation of molecular (DNA and protein) databases, A description of every step of molecular phylogenetic reconstruction, with a list of relevant bioinformatic tools, A presentation of diverse evolutionary analyses that can be performed from phylogenies, including time calibration, ancestral state reconstruction, genome evolution etc., with a list of relevant bioinformatic tools. Introduction to phylogenetic trees : concepts and definitions Retracing the evolution of species, genes and proteins, usually requires reconstructing a phylogenetic tree. A phylogenetic tree or phylogeny is a graphical representation of the evolutionary relationship between taxa or genes/proteins. Mathematically, a phylogenetic tree is a connected acyclic graph . The shape of the tree is known as topology . The taxa or sequences are positioned at the extremity of the branches and are sometimes referred to as "leaves". Groups of related organisms are known as OTU s (operational taxonomic units). For instance, genera are OTUs. Internal nodes , also referred to as HTUs (hypothetical taxomonic units), indicate the most recent common ancestors between taxa. In phylogenetic analysis, ancestors are hypothetical, nodes never indicate an identified extant or extinct species. A species ( e.g. Archaeopteryx lithographica or Tiktaalik rosaea ) is never considered the direct ancestor of a taxomomic group ( e.g. birds or tetrapods). Furthermore, only one route is possible from an ancestor to a descendant, as horizontal transfers, although common in microorganisms, are usually ignored. Ideally, every node is followed by a bipartition . In this case, the tree is said to be resolved . If the evolutionary relationships between some taxa cannot be determined, the tree will include polytomies , meaning that the tree is not fully resolved. The root of a phylogeny is the hypothetical common ancestor to all species or sequences in the tree. For instance, LUCA (last universal common ancestor), LECA (last eukaryotic common ancestor), Urmetazoa and Urbilateria are the hypothetical common ancestors of all living organisms, all eukaryotes, all animals and all bilaterians, respectively. In molecular phylogenies, ancestors are hypothetical ancestral genes or peoteins. Phylogenetic trees can be rooted if the root is indicated, or unrooted if not. Phylogenetic trees can consider branch lengths ( phylograms ) or not ( cladograms ). In the former, that take into account different evolution speeds, branch lengths can vary. In the latter, all branch lengths are equal. Modern biological classification is based on phylogenetic trees and species evolutionary relatedness. Nowadays, only groups including an ancestor and all its descendants, known as monophyletic groups or clades , are considered. Paraphyletic groups , that include an ancestor and only one part of its desendants (e.g. protozoa or fish), and polyphetic groups , that include several taxa but not their last common ancestor, are excluded in modern classification. Phylogenic analysis uses characters to retrace evolutionary relationships. They can be morphological or molecular. Molecular data are usually preferred on extant species. In molecular phylogenetics, the characters are nucleotides (A, T, G, C) or aminoacids (the 20 proteinogenic aminoacids) that constitute gene or protein sequences. Characters can be ancestral or derived , and only the phylogenetic analysis can determine the orientation. Only derived characters define monophyletic groups. Ancestral characters defie paraphyletic groups, and they are not relevant for classifications because they are not phylogenetically informative. Characters can also result from convergent evolution, creating homoplasy . Overview of phylogenetic analysis We describe the protocol from sequence harvesting from databases to phylogenetic tree building and diverse evolutionary studies. Our protocol can be summerized as follows: Protocol for the bioinformatic study of molecular phylogeny and evolution

Maximum parsimony (MP) Maximum parsimony is a classical and simple method, that calculates the minimum number of evolutionary steps, including nucleotide insertions, deletions or substitutions, between species. However, this method ignores hidden mutations and does not consider branch lengths, potentially leading to long branch attraction, an incorrect clustering of unrelated taxa. Furthermore, it does not consider the possibility of hidden mutations, making it not relevant for distant taxa. While MP is still used for morphological data, it is rarely used for molecular data. Method

Tree drawing Once the phylogenetic tree is computed, it can be exported using e.g. Newick file format and visualized using a graphical software such as FigTree , ETE Toolkit or ITOL . MEGA and SeaView also include visualization tools. Using different sets of options, several types of phylogenetic trees can be drawn (rooted or not, cladogram or phylogram), and branch support values (bootstrap values or posterior probabilities) can be displayed. Tools for graphical visualization and annotation of phylogenetic trees ETE Toolkit : Visualization and analysis of phylogenetic trees FigTree : Graphic software for phylogenetic trees ITOL *: Visualization and annotation of phylogenetic trees MEGA and Seaview include tree visualization and annotation tools With Mega 11: >Click " file " > " export current tree (Newick) ", select " Bootstrap " and " branch length ", retrieve the phylogenetic tree in the Newick format and save it with nwk as filename extention. With IQ-TREE 2: >Paste the phylogenetic tree in the Newick format to Notepad, and save it using nwk as filename extension. > Use a program (e.g. FigTree) in the list below and open the nwk files. You can also directly paste the phylogeny in the Newick format in the graphical tools. >Many options of tree drawing are available. For example, you can display the bootstrap values, the posterior probabilities, or the SH-aLRT values, collapse clades below a certain bootstrap threshold (e.g. 50), and highlight or add color to the clades. In our example (figure below), we used ITOL for the graphical representation of the phylogenetic tree of the P53 family. Interpretation of a phylogenetic tree Both methods reveal four major clades containing respectively the p53 of insects and the p53, p63, and p73 of all vertebrates. The p53, p63, and p73 of vertebrates are more closely related to each other than to any other p53. Furthermore, the p63 and p73 of vertebrates are more closely related to each other than to vertebrate p53. This indicates that two duplication events in the p53 family preceded the origin of vertebrates. First, the p53 family and the p63/p73 cluster diverged. The second one caused the p63 and p73 families to diverge. The p53 of insects are clustered together. This indicates that insects diverged from the other bilaterians before these two duplications. Phylogenetic trees of p53 domain-containing proteins of metazoans using Neighbour Joining (A) and Maximum Likelihood (B) . The trees were realized according to the model JTT+G, as calculated by ModelFinder using AIC. The numbers indicate the bootstrap values as calculated by the standard bootstrapping method and UFBoot2, respectively. The phylogenetic trees were inferred using MEGA 11 and IQ-TREE 2, respectively, and the figures were generated using ITOL. Green branches represent the p63 family, orange branches represent the p73 family and blue branches represent the p53 family.

Phylogenetic methods The evolutionary history of genes, proteins or species is generally presented as a phylogenetic tree, a graphical illustration of the evolutionary relationships between the sequences or taxa. Several methods for phylogenetic inference can be used: Method 1: Maximum parsimony (MP) Maximum parsimony is a classical and simple method, that calculates the minimum number of evolutionary steps, including nucleotide insertions, deletions or substitutions, between species. However, this method ignores hidden mutations and does not consider branch lengths, potentially leading to long branch attraction, an incorrect clustering of unrelated taxa. Furthermore, it does not consider the possibility of hidden mutations, making it not relevant for distant taxa. While MP is still used for morphological data, it is rarely used for molecular data. Method 2: Distance-based methods Distance-based methods create a matrix of molecular distances based on the number of differences between the sequences, to reconstruct the phylogenetic tree. These methods ignore hidden mutations and are also subject to long branch attraction. Distance-based methods include the Unweighted Pair Group Method with Arithmetic mean ( UPGMA ), Neighbor Joining ( NJ ), and Minimum Evolution ( ME ). Method 3: Probabilistic methods (requires selection of the molecular evolution model, see below) The strength of probabilistic methods is the use of specified models of molecular evolution. Probabilistic methods consider different mutation rates between sites to avoid mutation saturation. Nowadays, most studies of phylogenetic reconstruction use probabilistic methods. They include Maximum Likelihood ( ML , described below in the section Option 3-1) and Bayesian Inference ( BI , described below in the section Option 3-2). ML calculates the probability of observing the data (in this case, the sequence alignment) under different explicit models of molecular evolution. ML aims to identify the best fit model by exploring multiple combinations of model parameters. Inversely, BI evaluates the probability of each model of molecular evolution given the data. > Choose one or several phylogenetic methods to reconstruct the evolutionary history of your gene, protein or species of interest. It can be interesting to combine several approaches and compare the results (e.g. Maximum Likelihood, Neighbor Joining and Bayesian Inference). However, confirming phylogenetic relationships with several methods does not necessarily mean that the tree is biologically correct. Tools for phylogenetic reconstruction using diverse methods: MEGA : Sequence alignment, model selection, phylogenetic analysis using distance methods, MP and ML, and other evolutionary analyses. Complete and very user-friendly APE : R-written package for molecular phylogenetics FastMe *: Phylogenetic inference PHYLIP : Phylogenetic inference using MP, distance methods and ML Bayesian inference (BI) MrBayes : Phylogenetic inference using BI and diverse evolutionary analyses BAli-Phy : Phylogenetic inference BayesTraits : Phylogenetic inference and other evolutionary analyses PhyloBayes : Phylogenetic inference with protein data using BI using a specific probabilistic model Maximum likelyhood (ML) HYPHY *: Phylogenetic inference using ML and distance methods IQ-TREE *: Phylogenetic inference using ML, including model selection and a very fast bootstrapping method MEGA : Sequence alignment, model selection, phylogenetic analysis using distance methods, MP and ML, and other evolutionary analyses. Complete and very user-friendly. PAML : phylogenetic inference using ML, and other evolutionary analyses PAUP : Phylogenetic inference using MP and ML PHYLIP : Phylogenetic inference using MP, distance methods and ML PhyML *: Phylogenetic inference using ML and various evolutionary analyses RAxML *: Phylogenetic inference using ML SeaView : Sequence alignment and phylogenetic inference using MP, NJ and ML GARLI : Phylogenetic inference using ML Other : PyCogent : Phylogenetic inference and various evolutionary analyses SplitsTree : Phylogenetic inference for unrooted trees and phylogenetic networks > We propose to reconstruct the phylogeny of the TP53 family using a distance method: Neighbor Joining (NJ) with MEGA 11 , and a probabilistic method: Maximum Likelihood (ML) using IQ-TREE 2 .

steps.title: Collect gene or protein sequences
steps.instruction: Gather the required DNA or protein sequences from public databases in FASTA format.

substeps.instruction: Search for the gene or protein of interest (e.g., human TP53) in NCBI, Ensembl, UniProt, EMBL, InterPro, Prosite, or any listed database (NCBI, Ensembl, BAR, Bgee, GeneCards, FlyBase, PomBase, TAIR, WormBase, Xenbase, CATH, FSSP, Gene Ontology, KEGG, PDB, Pfam, PHAROS, PRINTS, PROSITE, SCOP, SUPERFAMILY, UniProt).
For UniProt, locate the accession (e.g., HsTP53 = P04637) and click “Sequence and Isoforms” to view the FASTA entry.
For NCBI, select the “Nucleotide” database, enter the gene name or GI number, click FASTA to view the sequence.
To batch‑download many sequences, use Ensembl BioMart, NCBI Batch Entrez, or UniProt Retrieve/ID‑mapping tools (provide URLs).
If needed, use Pfam batch download to retrieve all protein sequences from a genome.
Copy each FASTA entry (including the header line beginning with ">") into a plain‑text editor (e.g., Notepad) and save the file with a .fasta extension.

steps.title: Identify homologous sequences
steps.instruction: Find orthologous, paralogous and xenologous sequences using similarity searches and download them in FASTA format.

substeps.instruction: Open the NCBI BLAST web page (https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi).
Paste the FASTA sequence of the query (human TP53) into the query box.

Run BLAST (protein or nucleotide as appropriate) against genomes of the chosen taxa (e.g., Hydra vulgaris, Drosophila melanogaster, Bombus terrestris, Apis mellifera, Aedes aegyptus, Ciona intestinalis, Danio rerio, Latimeria chalumnae, Xenopus tropicalis, Anolis carolinensis, Gallus gallus, Bos taurus, Homo sapiens).
Filter results by E‑value (significant) and by ≥30 % sequence identity.
For vertebrate species, select one sequence for each paralogue (p53, p63, p73).
Download all selected sequences as a single FASTA file.
Optional: compute a percent‑identity matrix with CLUSTALW 2.1 to inspect similarity levels (e.g., human paralogues 36‑100 % identity, Monosiga brevicollis orthologues 17‑25 % identity).

steps.title: Perform multiple sequence alignment
steps.instruction: Align all collected sequences using an MSA program and save the alignment.

substeps.instruction: Open the MAFFT web server (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/Tools/msa/mafft/).
Paste the FASTA file containing all homologues into the input box.
Use the default parameters (including default gap‑opening penalty).
Submit the job, retrieve the resulting alignment in FASTA format, and save it as a new .fasta file (the “full‑MSA”).

steps.title: Trim the alignment
steps.instruction: Remove poorly aligned or highly variable regions to obtain a phylogenetically informative sub‑MSA.

substeps.instruction: Upload the full‑MSA to the Guidance 2 server (http://guidance.tau.ac.il/).
Run Guidance 2 with default settings (or choose a column‑score cutoff).
Inspect the colour‑coded alignment; manually delete columns with low scores or let Guidance 2 output a trimmed alignment.
Save the trimmed alignment as a new FASTA file (the “sub‑MSA”).
Alternative tools (AliStat, BMGE, GBlocks, Noisy, TrimAl) may be used similarly.

steps.title: Classify protein domains (optional)
steps.instruction: Retrieve domain classifications for the protein of interest and visualise their taxonomic distribution.

substeps.instruction: Open Pfam (https://pfam.xfam.org/) and search for the protein (e.g., PF00870 for p53).
Record the four main domains (P53 TAD, P53 TAD2, P53 DNA‑binding domain, P53 tetramer) and note that the DNA‑binding domain spans amino acids 99‑289.
Note the number of domain‑containing sequences: 1 765 sequences from 382 species (5 choanoflagellates, 13 human).
Retrieve the sunburst plot of domain occurrence by clicking “Sequences” on the right.
Open SCOP (https://scop.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/) and record the hierarchy for the p53 DNA‑binding domain (Class b, Fold b.2, Superfamily b.2.5, Family b.2.5.2).

steps.title: Select best‑fit evolutionary model
steps.instruction: Determine the optimal substitution model for the protein alignment using model‑selection software.

substeps.instruction: Launch ProtTest 3.4.2 and load the sub‑MSA.
Run the analysis on the full set of 56 amino‑acid models; record the log‑likelihoods.
Select the model with the lowest BIC or AIC (e.g., JTT+G if that is the best).
Alternatively, use IQ‑TREE ModelFinder (http://iqtree.cibiv.univie.ac.at/) or MEGA’s “Find best DNA/Protein models” panel with the same criterion.

steps.title: Reconstruct phylogeny with MP
steps.instruction: Build a maximum‑parsimony tree in MEGA 11 and assess support.

substeps.instruction: Open MEGA 11 and import the sub‑MSA.
In the Phylogeny panel, choose “Maximum Parsimony”.
Set the bootstrap option to at least 1 000 replicates.
Run the analysis and save the resulting tree.

steps.title: Reconstruct phylogeny with NJ
steps.instruction: Build a neighbour‑joining tree in MEGA 11 using the selected model.

substeps.instruction: Import the sub‑MSA into MEGA 11.
Select “Neighbour‑Joining” in the Phylogeny panel.
Choose the substitution model identified in step 6 (e.g., JTT+G).
Set bootstrap replicates to ≥1 000.
Execute the run and save the tree.

steps.title: Reconstruct phylogeny with ML
steps.instruction: Perform maximum‑likelihood inference using IQ‑TREE 2 with ultrafast bootstrapping.

substeps.instruction: Upload the sub‑MSA to the IQ‑TREE web server (http://iqtree.cibiv.univie.ac.at/).
Select “Protein sequences”, choose the model from step 6 (e.g., JTT+G).
In the Branch Support panel, enable “Ultrafast Bootstrap” with ≥1 000 replicates and optionally the SH‑aLRT test.
Run the analysis, download the tree file (Newick) and the log file.

steps.title: Root the phylogenetic tree
steps.instruction: Define an outgroup or apply midpoint rooting to the inferred tree.

substeps.instruction: In the tree‑editing program, designate Monosiga brevicollis p53 as the outgroup (or add a second, more distant outgroup).
Alternatively, select “Midpoint rooting” if no explicit outgroup is used.

steps.title: Calibrate tree with divergence times
steps.instruction: Add fossil or molecular clock calibration points using MEGA 11 and TimeTree.

substeps.instruction: In MEGA 11, open the alignment and the Newick tree.
Choose Compute → Compute Timetree.
Move Monosiga brevicollis to the Outgroups panel.
Select “Internal nodes constraints”.
Visit TimeTree (http://www.timetree.org/), enter two species (e.g., Homo and Drosophila) to obtain a median divergence of 694 Myr (range 630‑830 Myr).
In MEGA, click “Add new calibration point”, select the corresponding node, and enter the median age (or min/max).
Repeat for additional calibration points as desired.
Launch the analysis, then export the calibrated tree with divergence times.

steps.title: Reconstruct ancestral sequences
steps.instruction: Infer ancestral states for each node using MEGA 11.

substeps.instruction: Import the sub‑MSA and the calibrated tree into MEGA 11.
Open the Ancestors panel and choose “Infer ancestral sequences”.
Select the inference method (Maximum Parsimony or Maximum Likelihood).
If ML is chosen, confirm the substitution model from step 6.
Run the analysis and view the reconstructed sequences at each node.

steps.title: Estimate selection pressure (dN/dS)
steps.instruction: Calculate nonsynonymous/synonymous substitution ratios with MEGA 11.

substeps.instruction: Load the protein‑coding alignment and the phylogenetic tree into MEGA 11.
Open the Selection panel and choose “Compute dN/dS”.
Interpret results: dN/dS > 1 indicates positive selection.

steps.title: Analyse co‑evolution of protein families
steps.instruction: Create a nexus file and run co‑evolution analyses with Jane and TreeMap.

substeps.instruction: Create a text file beginning with “#NEXUS”.

Add three blocks: BEGIN HOST; (list cyclin tree in Newick); END; BEGIN PARASITE; (list CDK tree in Newick); END; BEGIN DISTRIBUTION; list each host‑parasite association as “Host:Parasite,”; END; finally add “ENDBLOCK;”.
Import the nexus file into Jane, select Solve Mode, set event costs, and run the analysis (stats mode optional).
Import the same file into TreeMap, choose “Solve the tanglegram”, run, and optionally test significance.
